# Tŷ Mawr — The Great House Farm Story — llms.txt

> The true story of the Williams/Buckler family and Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough-juxta-Penarth, Vale of Glamorgan, Wales, in 162 scenes across 9 acts with a prologue and epilogue, in strict date order.
> Every scene is drawn from the Great House Farm Wiki evidence catalogue (https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/) and carries its evidence links.
> Structured JSON (acts, cast, scenes, evidence, stable ids): https://bpvsbuckler.bucklerfamily.estate/api/timeline.json
> Printable script (static HTML, no JavaScript needed): https://bpvsbuckler.bucklerfamily.estate/story/
> Storyboard: https://bpvsbuckler.bucklerfamily.estate/?view=storyboard · Cast: https://bpvsbuckler.bucklerfamily.estate/?view=cast · Any scene: https://bpvsbuckler.bucklerfamily.estate/?event=<id>

## About

The Williams family lived at Great House Farm, Llandough, for generations (per the Buckler case, since 1667). The family's case is that the farm was two parcels: the house parcel (Parcel A), which passed out of the Bute estate to Daniel Thomas in 1877 and became the family's freehold when quarrying ended in 1928, and the eastern fields (Parcel B), which went to Western Ground Rents in 1938 and to BP. The possession cases of 1955, 1962, 1974 and BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 decided possession; none of them examined the documents that bear on the family's title to the house parcel. BP demolished the farmhouse on 6 December 1988, the morning after Cadw declined to list it, before it could be fully recorded. In 1994 an early-medieval cemetery of 1,026 burials was excavated on the site. Since 2025 the family have been recovering the missing records, and Cadw, Heneb and HM Land Registry's Independent Complaints Reviewer are now investigating. The family's case is that fraud and concealment kept the title documents from the courts, so the case can be reopened.

Truth labels follow the Wiki: documented fact, testimony only (named witness), reconstruction, legal inference and unresolved. The 1978–79 Llandough Roman Villa is a separate archaeological site, distinct from Great House Farm.

## Full Timeline

162 scenes, in strict date order.

### P.1 (1). Late Iron Age (approx. 2,200 years ago; exact date uncertain) — Iron Age farmstead at Llandough

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-02000101-1 · Parcel: Not Great House Farm land · Basis: Archaeological record

Excavations in 1978–79 at the separate Llandough Roman Villa site identified earlier Iron Age occupation. A curvilinear feature and postholes may represent a round hut; associated pottery is in a late Iron Age tradition. This is evidence for early occupation at Llandough, not evidence that a round hut stood on the Great House Farm parcel.

> What we now know: Heneb's record for the separate Llandough Roman Villa site describes an Iron Age farmstead and a possible round hut, represented by a curvilinear feature and postholes. The pottery indicates a pre-Conquest tradition, but the record does not establish an exact date of c. 200 BC or show that the hut stood on Great House Farm itself.
- Heritage record: Heneb HER GGAT00768s — Llandough Roman Villa (Iron Age farmstead / possible round hut) — https://archwilio.org.uk/her/chi3/report/page.php?watprn=GGAT00768s
- National monument record: Coflein NPRN 400051 — Roman Villa Site, Llandough; excavation in 1979 — https://coflein.gov.uk/en/site/400051/

### P.2 (2). c. 650 (approximate) — St Dochdwy's

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-06500101-1 · Date: 0650-01-01 · Parcel: Not Great House Farm land · Basis: Archaeological record

Beside the farm stands St Dochdwy's, Llandough. It is thought to have been an early monastery, founded around the year 650; the churchyard and the ground north of it hold the burials later excavated in 1994.

> What we now know: The church and its early burial ground sit next to the farm; the 1994 cemetery excavation north of the church took place on former farm land.
- Heritage record: Archaeology and Heritage — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/archaeology/
- Heritage record: Historic Environment Record GGAT 02038s (Archwilio) — https://archwilio.org.uk/her/chi3/report/page.php?watprn=GGAT02038s

### P.3 (3). 12th – 14th century — Medieval occupation

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-12000101-1 · Date: 1200-01-01 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Archaeological record

In 1962–63 E. J. Beare reports pottery of the 12th to 14th centuries on the slope north-east of the house. The Royal Commission classes the house as sub-medieval, probably 17th century, possibly with a medieval core.

> The received account: An old farmhouse of no special note.
> Wording: "sub-medieval" — A technical dating term, later read as "not old enough to matter".
> What we now know: A house of the 17th century or earlier, on a site occupied since the Middle Ages, possibly with a medieval core.
- Heritage record: Historic Environment Record GGAT 02038s (Archwilio) — https://archwilio.org.uk/her/chi3/report/page.php?watprn=GGAT02038s
- Heritage record: Archaeology and Heritage — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/archaeology/
- Analysis: GGAT — Forensic Review — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/scrutiny-and-accountability/government-public-authority-involvement/ggat-forensic-review-and-evidence-schedule-v4-0-3/

### P.4 (4). 1536 – 1793 — The lordship of the manor

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-15450101-1 · Date: 1545-01-01 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Public record

Llandough belongs to Tewkesbury Abbey until the Dissolution of 1536–39. Cardiff Records states that in 1543 Henry VIII granted the manor to Lord Clynton and Say and Robert Turwitt, and that by 1545 it was held by Sir George Herbert. The Western Mail letter states that the Herberts held the lordship until the Earl of Bute bought it in 1793; Cardiff Records places William Hurst and others in the account from 1767. The same 1974 newspaper record identifies Mary (Nancy) Williams's family as occupying the manorial home since 1667. That occupation and the lordship are separate from the farmhouse freehold. The family's case is that the Williamses were virtual freeholders under the 1877 bargain while quarrying continued, and that Parcel A's freehold passed to them in 1928 when quarrying ended.

> The received account: The lord of the manor owned the farm.
> Wording: "since 1667" — The 1974 newspaper records the Williams family’s occupation of the manorial home; occupation is a separate matter from the lordship and the freehold.
> What we now know: Lordship of a manor and ownership of the farmhouse parcel are separate interests. The 1974 newspaper records the Williams family’s occupation of the manorial home since 1667. The family’s title case is not occupation alone: it is that the 1877 bargain entitled the Williamses to Parcel A’s freehold when quarrying ended, identified by Mary as 1928, when the final rent was paid. On that account, the Williamses were virtual freeholders while the quarrying arrangement ran and became freeholders in 1928. The 1877 deed and final receipt have not been located, so the 1928 transfer remains the family’s asserted title history rather than a fact determined by the 1974 newspaper or a court. The manorial sources also differ over 1767–1793; the Herbert estate papers have not yet been checked.
> Title move — Great House (one farm): Lordship of the manor: Sir George Herbert (by 1545) and his family

- Newspaper: Western Mail, 'Grievous loss' (1974 letter giving manorial descent and the Williams occupation) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/press-archive-transcripts/#n04
- Mary's statement: Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement (c. 1974) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/mary-williams-statement/
- Wiki page: The 1877 Agreement — the sale — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1877-agreement/#sale-1877
- Wiki page: The 1877 Agreement — takes effect in 1928 — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1877-agreement/#takes-effect
- Wiki page: Llandough (Penarth): Cydfin / Tŷ Mawr and pre-1877 manorial evidence — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/anomalies-register/llandough-penarth-cydfin-ty-mawr-manorial-evidence/

### P.5 (5). 20 June 1547 — A 1,000-year lease of Cydwin

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-15470620-1 · Date: 1547-06-20 · Parcel: Not yet known · Basis: Archival catalogue

The National Library of Wales catalogue describes a lease for 1,000 years dated 20 June 1547 from Sir George Herbert of Swansea to Edmund Vaughan of a farm called Cydwin in the manor of Llandough; the record names fields. This long leasehold interest predates the later Bute estate narrative. The affirmative Cedwyn thesis asks whether those named fields belong to the older Cydfin/Ty Mawr holding later catalogued as a 107-acre farm, and how that interest passed from the Herbert/Vaughan line into subsequent estate records. The instrument and field boundaries must be examined before the lease can be equated with the whole Great House site.

> The received account: The Bute estate is the beginning of the land's title.
> What we now know: The 1547 NLW catalogue entry names a Cydwin farm in the manor of Llandough and a 1,000-year lease from Sir George Herbert to Edmond Vaughan. That is a specific pre-Bute interest and an archival route to follow. It does not yet identify every field with the later Great House boundaries; the lease and its named fields must be compared with D 219 and historic plans.
- Archive catalogue: National Library of Wales, L 11 — assignment of a lease for 1,000 years of Cydwin in the manor of Llandough — https://archifau.llyfrgell.cymru/index.php/assignment-of-lease-for-1000-years-of-cydwin-in-manor-of-llandough
- Estate papers: National Library of Wales, Bute Estate Records D 219 — Llandough manorial leases and agreements — https://archives.library.wales/index.php/llandough-manorial-leases-and-agreements
- Wiki page: GHF-E178 — 1547 Cydwin lease lead — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/ghf-e173-cedwyn-cwm-cedwyn-place-name-notes/ghf-e178-1547-sir-george-herbert-grants-vaughan-a-1000-year-lease-of-cydwin/
- Wiki page: Llandough (Penarth): Cydfin / Tŷ Mawr and pre-1877 manorial evidence — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/anomalies-register/llandough-penarth-cydfin-ty-mawr-manorial-evidence/
- Research annex: Cedwyn Estate — title-chain reconstruction — https://bpvsbuckler.bucklerfamily.estate/research/cedwyn-estate-title-chain.html

### P.6 (6). 1552 – 1824 — Manorial leases

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-15520101-1 · Date: 1552-01-01 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Estate papers

The National Library of Wales holds a Bute Estate bundle of Llandough manorial leases and agreements (D 219), dated 1552–1829 as a whole. Its catalogue identifies leases of "Cydfin Farm or Ty Mawr Farm, (107 a.)", dated 1552–1824.

> The received account: A farm let on ordinary leases.
> What we now know: The farm is on written record from 1552. The 1829 end date belongs to the bundle as a whole, not to the farm, and no event in 1829 is recorded. The individual deeds have not yet been inspected; they should show who granted the leases and on what terms.
> Title move — Great House (one farm): Farm (Cydfin or Tŷ Mawr, 107 acres): leases on record 1552–1824 · lordship of the manor: the Herberts

- Estate papers: National Library of Wales, Bute Estate Records D 219: Llandough manorial leases and agreements, 1552–1829 — https://archives.library.wales/index.php/llandough-manorial-leases-and-agreements
- Wiki page: Name & Location Variations — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/great-house-farm/name-variations/

### P.7 (7). Mid 16th – late 18th century — The Vaughans

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-15600101-1 · Date: 1560-01-01 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Heritage record

From the mid-16th to the late 18th century the Vaughan family hold Great House as the chief freehold farm of the parish. The lordship of the manor is a separate interest, held over the same period by the Herberts.

> The received account: One chain of owners: the Herberts, then the Vaughans, then Bute.
> What we now know: Two separate lines. The lordship of the manor: Tewkesbury Abbey, the Crown, the Herberts from 1545, Bute from 1793. The ownership of the farm: a freehold within the manor, held by the Vaughans until the late 18th century and by Bute from the early 19th. How the farm passed from the Vaughans to Bute is not yet documented. Parcel A's title descends from the farm freehold, not from the lordship.
> Title move — Great House (one farm): Farm freehold: the Vaughans · lordship of the manor: the Herberts (a separate interest)

- Heritage record: Historic Environment Record GGAT 02038s (Archwilio) — https://archwilio.org.uk/her/chi3/report/page.php?watprn=GGAT02038s
- Wiki page: The Bute Estate (Vaughan chief freehold farm) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/bute-estate/
- Wiki page: 1990 GGAT Assessment — transcription (Vaughan phase) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1990-ggat-archaeological-assessment-great-house-farm-llandough-transcription/

### P.8 (8). 1667 — The Williams family at Great House

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-16670101-1 · Date: 1667-01-01 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Mary's statement

Mary (Nancy) Williams's c.1974 statement records that her family had lived and farmed at Great House since 1667. A 1974 newspaper report also reports her statement that her family first acquired Tŷ Mawr around that date. The affirmative Cedwyn thesis treats 1667 as the opening of the family's own estate history and tests that statement against the Cydwin/Cydfin lease and farm-name records. The surviving statement and press report support the Buckler case; a 1667 conveyance has not yet been identified.

> The received account: Tenant farmers who lived on someone else's land.
> Wording: "tenants" — The estate's description of the family, repeated in every later account.
> What we now know: Mary's statement and the 1974 press report support the Buckler case for a connection with Great House from 1667 and treat it as a lineage claim, not a passing tenancy. The affirmative reconstruction now connects that claim to the older Cydwin/Cydfin/Ty Mawr lease records and asks whether later labels of tenancy concealed a longer-standing family interest. The surviving items do not themselves constitute a 1667 conveyance; the deed chain must be reconstructed from the leases, estate accounts, plans and the 1877/1928 evidence.
> Title move — Great House (one farm): Farm freehold: the Vaughans · lordship of the manor: the Herberts · in the house: the Williamses

- Mary's statement: Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement (c. 1974) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/mary-williams-statement/
- Wiki page: The Williams / Buckler Family — origins — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/williams-buckler-family/

### P.9 (9). 13 February 1739/40 — Vaughan assigns the Cydwin lease

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-17400213-1 · Date: 1740-02-13 · Parcel: Not yet known · Basis: Archival catalogue

The National Library of Wales catalogues an assignment dated 13 February 1739/40 by Edmond Vaughan of Llandough to Thomas Mathews of Llandaf of the 1,000-year Cydwin lease originally granted in 1547, for £1,066 13s. 4d. This is a documented transfer in the older lease chain and a concrete route for tracing who held the interest before Bute's later estate records. The next step is to match the named fields and follow subsequent assignments, rentals and conveyances into the Cydfin/Ty Mawr farm and the later parcels.

> The received account: The Vaughan lease chain has no relevance once later estate papers call the land Ty Mawr.
> What we now know: The L 11 catalogue records Edmond Vaughan's 1739/40 assignment of the 1,000-year Cydwin lease to Thomas Mathews for £1,066 13s. 4d. The assignment offers a concrete transfer point for reconstructing the older interest. Follow its named fields and later assignments into the Cydfin/Ty Mawr records and the eventual Bute estate acquisition.
- Archive catalogue: National Library of Wales, L 11 — assignment of a lease for 1,000 years of Cydwin in the manor of Llandough — https://archifau.llyfrgell.cymru/index.php/assignment-of-lease-for-1000-years-of-cydwin-in-manor-of-llandough
- Estate papers: National Library of Wales, Bute Estate Records D 219 — Llandough manorial leases and agreements — https://archives.library.wales/index.php/llandough-manorial-leases-and-agreements
- Wiki page: GHF-E179 — Cydfin / Ty Mawr names in Bute records — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/ghf-e173-cedwyn-cwm-cedwyn-place-name-notes/ghf-e179-1552-1824-bute-records-call-it-cedfin-cydfin-ken-fin-farm-or-ty-mawr-farm/
- Research annex: Cedwyn Estate — title-chain reconstruction — https://bpvsbuckler.bucklerfamily.estate/research/cedwyn-estate-title-chain.html

### P.10 (10). 1793 – early 19th century — The Bute Estate

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-18000101-1 · Date: 1800-01-01 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Heritage record

The historical account places Bute's acquisition of the lordship of Llandough in 1793 and its acquisition of the Great House freehold in the early 19th century; the manorial courts of Llandough and Leckwith were held at the house. The missing control point is the instrument that carried the farm freehold from the Vaughan line into Bute's estate. The 1547 Cydwin lease, its 1739/40 assignment, and the D 219 record of Cydfin or Ty Mawr leases give the affirmative reconstruction a named chain to investigate alongside the manor's later ownership. A manorial interest, a long lease, and a farm freehold must be mapped separately before the later corporate titles can be treated as the originating chain for every parcel.

> The received account: Bute owned the farm, and everything after descends from Bute.
> What we now know: The historical account places the manorial lordship in Bute's hands from 1793 and the Great House farm freehold in the early 19th century. The deed that moved the farm freehold from the Vaughan line is the key missing control point. The L 11 lease assignment and D 219 farm records provide older property and tenure references against which Bute's acquisition, rentals and subsequent 1877 division must be tested. The house was also a centre for the Llandough and Leckwith manorial courts; that administrative role must not be confused with ownership of each parcel.
> Title move — Great House (one farm): Lordship of the manor (1793) and farm freehold (early 19th century): the Bute Estate · tenants: the Williamses

- Heritage record: Historic Environment Record GGAT 02038s (Archwilio) — https://archwilio.org.uk/her/chi3/report/page.php?watprn=GGAT02038s
- Wiki page: The Bute Estate — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/bute-estate/
- Wiki page: Llandough (Penarth): Cydfin / Tŷ Mawr and pre-1877 manorial evidence — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/anomalies-register/llandough-penarth-cydfin-ty-mawr-manorial-evidence/
- Estate papers: National Library of Wales, Bute Estate Records R1: Glamorgan Estate rentals — https://archives.library.wales/index.php/glamorgan-estate-rentals
- Wiki page: Name & Location Variations (Stewart survey, D/d B E/1–2) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/great-house-farm/name-variations/

### P.11 (11). c. 1840 — Great House Farm

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-18400101-1 · Date: 1840-01-01 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Public record

Census and tithe records begin to describe the house as "Great House Farm".

> The received account: It was always just a farm.
> Wording: "Great House Farm" — A name that reduced the manor's court house to a farmhouse.
> What we now know: The first change in how the place was described. Later descriptions, especially "the whole farm", decide the case.
- Wiki page: Farmhouse Nomenclature — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/great-house-farm/farmhouse-nomenclature/
- Wiki page: Name & Location Variations — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/great-house-farm/name-variations/

### P.12 (12). 1855 — John Williams succeeds his father

Prologue: To 1857 · Scene id: ghf-18550101-1 · Date: 1855-01-01 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Newspaper

John Williams succeeds his father as occupier of the farm under the Bute Estate. Reporting the Bute rent audit dinner of July 1904, the Cardiff Times reports that he "succeeded his father in the tenancy of the farm in 1855", and that it was "his 102nd rent audit".

> What we now know: One newspaper line, written 49 years later, gives 1855 as the start of John Williams's tenancy and says he took it over from his father; the 1841 tithe already has a John Williams holding about 120 acres at Tŷ Mawr. Against it: the 1904 report calls him "of Llandough Farm", the name of the Rees family's separate farm, so reading it as Great House rests on the directories, which put him at "Great House" in 1891 and 1901 (an inference, not proof). The Bute rent audits that would confirm 1855 have not been seen.
- Newspaper: Cardiff Times, 16 July 1904, p.1 — Bute rent audit dinner (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3427270/3427271/13/
- Newspaper: EV-0227 — Cardiff Times, 16 July 1904: John Williams, tenancy since 1855 (wiki evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0227-cardiff-times-1904-john-williams-tenancy-since-1855/
- Wiki page: EV-0215 — Tithe apportionment: John Williams, c. 1841 — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0215-tithe-apportionment-john-williams-c1841/

### I.1 (13). 23 December 1864 — Death of Amy Williams of Great House

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18641223-1 · Date: 1864-12-23 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Newspaper

Amy Williams dies at Llandough, aged 65. The death notices call her "relict of the late Mr. John Williams, Great House farm": the widow of the elder John Williams, whose son John had taken over the tenancy in 1855.

> Wording: "relict of the late Mr. John Williams, Great House farm" — The notice's own words: the elder John Williams was dead by December 1864, and was remembered as "of Great House farm".
> What we now know: VERIFIED (two contemporary death notices, read on Welsh Newspapers Online). They fit the 1904 report that the younger John Williams "succeeded his father in the tenancy of the farm in 1855". Not yet found: the elder John Williams's own death or burial entry, and Amy's maiden name.
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Cardiff Times, 30 December 1864, p.5 — deaths: "at Llandough, near Cardiff, Amy, relict of the late Mr. John Williams, Great House farm, aged 65 years" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3383386/3383391/14/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Cardiff and Merthyr Guardian, 30 December 1864, p.5 — deaths: "WILLIAMS.—Dec. 23, at Llandough, near Cardiff, Amy, relict of the late Mr. John Williams, Great House farm, aged 65" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3094324/3094329/21/
- Newspaper: EV-0246 — the death notices on the wiki (evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0246-cardiff-times-1864-death-of-amy-williams-great-house-farm/

### I.2 (14). 1868 – 1901 — "Williams John, Great house"

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18680101-1 · Date: 1868-01-01 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Publication

The trade directories list the farmers of Llandough parish. Every edition from 1868 to 1901 has "Williams John, Great house", from 1887 "Great House farm, Llandough". Thomas Rees, and later Evan Rees, are listed separately, at Llandough Farm, a different Bute farm.

> What we now know: Six directories over 33 years put the same John Williams at Great House and the Rees family at Llandough Farm, so the two farms, and the two families, were distinct. Against it: directories copy from one edition to the next and record what the compiler was told; none uses the name "Home Farm"; and the press of 1895 and 1904 sometimes calls a Williams "of Llandough Farm", so that name in a source does not always mean the Rees farm.
- Publication: Slater's Directory 1868, p.902, Llandough: "Williams John, Great house" (University of Leicester Historical Directories) — https://leicester.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/91309
- Publication: Worrall's Directory 1875, p.324, farmers in Llandough parish: "Williams John, Great house" (University of Leicester Historical Directories) — https://leicester.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/348840
- Publication: Slater's Directory 1880, p.533, farmers in Llandough: "Williams John, Greathouse" (University of Leicester Historical Directories) — https://leicester.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/90316
- Publication: Owen's Cardiff Directory 1887, p.209: "Williams John, Great House farm, Llandough" (University of Leicester Historical Directories) — https://leicester.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/92950
- Publication: Owen's Cardiff Directory 1891, p.237: "Williams John, overseer, Great House farm, Llandough" (University of Leicester Historical Directories) — https://leicester.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/93394
- Publication: Cardiff Directory 1901, p.309: "Williams John, Great House farm, Llandough" (University of Leicester Historical Directories) — https://leicester.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/95085
- Publication: EV-0225 — Trade directories 1868–1901: "Williams John, Great house" (wiki evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0225-trade-directories-1868-1901-john-williams-great-house/
- Newspaper: Weekly Mail, 6 November 1886 — Thomas Rees, aged 89, of Llandough Farm, "rented from the Marquess of Bute" — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3365383/3365390/150/
- Newspaper: EV-0228 — Llandough Farm and the Rees family, 1841–1910: a separate Bute farm (wiki evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0228-llandough-farm-rees-family-1841-1910/

### I.3 (15). c. 1870 — The armour under the floor

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18700101-1 · Date: 1870-01-01 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Source pending

Family tradition records a soldier in armour, with his horse, a lance and a shield, found beneath the dining-room floor. The account is in a Royal Commission record (NMR 6048942) and the Daily Telegraph of 16 April 1974. No primary record of a find has been located.

> The received account: Family folklore.
> Wording: "reported" — The word the records use, which keeps it at a distance.
> What we now know: An account on public record since 1974, never investigated before the house was demolished.
- Newspaper: Daily Telegraph, 16 April 1974 (dates the find to "about 1870") — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/press-archive-transcripts/#n03
- Heritage record: Historic Environment Record GGAT 02038s (Archwilio) — https://archwilio.org.uk/her/chi3/report/page.php?watprn=GGAT02038s
- Heritage record: Archaeology and Heritage — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/archaeology/
- Analysis: Source Conflicts Register — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/records-access-chronology/source-conflicts-register/

### I.4 (16). 1870 — Pwllypant probate and estate papers — A Williams estate bequest to Bute: tracing the land

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18700101-2 · Date: 1870-01-02 · Parcel: Not yet known · Basis: Probate and estate catalogue leads

The National Library of Wales catalogue lists the 1870 will of William Evans Williams of Pwllypant as bequeathing his real and personal estate to the Marquis of Bute, and separately catalogues papers about his real and personal estate. The affirmative title inquiry is parcel-specific: did any land he owned, benefited from, or had let through Bute connect to the 33-acre Llandough Limeworks block or Great House Farm? The will's headline bequest does not identify those acres by itself. The family's research also points to a Clock Tower dispute and newspaper coverage that may have complicated the relationship between Williams and Bute; the precise contemporary reports and wording must be located before using that dispute as proof of motive. Estate schedules, title deeds, rent books and the 1876–1912 limeworks accounts are the route to answer the question.

> The received account: William Evans Williams left his fortune to Bute, so the land history is settled.
> What we now know: The catalogued 1870 will is a lead to the estate's disposition, not a parcel schedule for Great House Farm. Test whether land or rights connected with Llandough's 33-acre limeworks block appear in William Evans Williams's title papers, rentals or correspondence. The reported Clock Tower dispute should be linked to its exact contemporary newspaper source before it is used to characterise the relationship.
- Archive catalogue: National Library of Wales, D242/17 — probate of the will of William Evans Williams of Pwllypant (1870) — https://archives.library.wales/index.php/deeds-and-documents-relating-mainly-to-title-of-pwllypant-estate-including-copy-probate-of-will-of-david-evan%3Bisad?sf_culture=en
- Archive catalogue: National Library of Wales, D258 — papers relating to the personal and real estates of William Evans Williams — https://archives.library.wales/index.php/papers-relating-to-personal-and-real-estates-of-william-evans-williams-dec-including-account-of-aberdare-iron-co
- Historical context: History Points — Former Pwllypant House, Caerphilly — https://historypoints.org/index.php?page=former-pwllypant-house-caerphilly
- Wiki page: Llandough Limeworks — the 33-acre block — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/llandough-limeworks/
- Wiki page: The Bute Estate — unresolved early title — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/bute-estate/
- Research annex: Cedwyn Estate — title-chain reconstruction — https://bpvsbuckler.bucklerfamily.estate/research/cedwyn-estate-title-chain.html

### I.5 (17). 1876 – c. 1912 — The limeworks

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18760101-1 · Date: 1876-01-01 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Estate papers

The Wiki's archive lead identifies about 33 acres used by the Llandough Limeworks from 1876 to about 1912, with Bute papers D153/4–8 to be obtained and inspected. The block's precise boundaries and title line remain to be matched to the 1877 plan and the estate schedules. For the Cedwyn reconstruction, this is a critical parcel-control point: identify who owned the freehold, who granted the quarrying rights, who received rent, and whether all four descriptions refer to the same acres.

> The received account: Part of the farm let for quarrying.
> What we now know: The archive lead identifies a 33-acre quarrying block in Bute records from 1876 to about 1912, but its exact parcel and chain of authority need to be established from D153/4–8, the 1877 plan and the estate schedules. The key affirmative question is who held the underlying freehold and who merely let or administered the quarrying rights.
- Newspaper: EV-0280 — Llandough Lime Works and quarry, 1876–1947: contemporary record set — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0280-llandough-lime-works-and-quarry-1876-1947-daniel-thomas-s-kilns-quarry-workers-kel/
- Wiki page: Llandough Limeworks — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/llandough-limeworks/

### I.6 (18). 1877 — Division of the farm

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18770101-1 · Date: 1877-01-01 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Mary's statement

Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement records that in 1877 the Bute Estate sold the farmhouse, buildings and about 10 acres to Daniel Thomas, and kept about 9 acres. The Williamses remained the occupiers of both. The deed is missing.

> The received account: Nothing changed: Bute went on owning the farm, and the Williamses went on renting it.
> What we now know: On Mary's statement, from 1877 there are two parcels with two owners: Parcel A, the house, owned by Thomas; Parcel B, the fields, kept by Bute. Anything Bute sells after 1877 can only be Parcel B. Her statement says the freehold of the house was to pass to the Williamses when quarrying ended. The deed is missing; the wiki notes that whether the 1877 deal was a sale or a quarry lease is still to be tested against the Bute papers.
> Title move — Parcel A: the true title: Freehold: Daniel Thomas (bought from Bute) · tenants: the Williamses, promised the freehold when quarrying ends
> Title move — Parcel B: the fields: Freehold: the Bute Estate · tenants: the Williamses

- Archive catalogue: EV-0278 — NLW Bute records: Llandough manor rentals 1808–1881 and presentments 1793–1934 (catalogue entries) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0278-nlw-bute-estate-records-llandough-manor-rentals-1808-1881-r-6-27-45-and-presentmen/
- Mary's statement: Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement (c. 1974) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/mary-williams-statement/
- Wiki page: The 1877 Agreement — the sale — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1877-agreement/#sale-1877
- Wiki page: The 1877 Agreement — plan — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1877-agreement/#plan
- Wiki page: The Two Parcels — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/the-two-parcels/
- Wiki page: The 1877 Agreement — Bute lease — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1877-agreement/#sale-1877
- Analysis: Forensic Master Chronology (6 October 2026) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/forensic-master-chronology-authoritative-corrected-6-october-2026/

### I.7 (19). 3 April 1881 — The 1881 census: "Llandough Home Farm"

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18810403-1 · Date: 1881-04-03 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Public record

The 1881 census records "Llandough Home Farm": John Williams, 53, "Farmer of 170 [? or 120] ac. employing 1 man and 1 boy", born at Leckwith; his wife Mary, 51, born at Cogan; their children Ellen, 14, John, 13, and David, 9; a boarder and a servant. Per Sion Buckler, this is Great House Farm entered under the wrong name. The directories of 1880 and 1887 place the same John Williams at Great House.

> Wording: "Llandough Home Farm" — The enumerator's label. No other source found uses it: no newspaper (Welsh Newspapers Online, 1804–1919), directory or Ordnance Survey map.
> What we now know: The household is the John Williams whom the directories place at Great House before and after 1881. The Rees family were at Llandough Farm. On identity the record supports Sion Buckler's reading. Against it: "Home Farm" appears nowhere else, so it cannot be offered as a second name for the farm; and the acreage is hard to read: 170 would fit Llandough Farm (166 acres in 1824–32) better than Great House (about 120 acres in the 1841 tithe), while 120 fits Great House. Folio and enumeration district: source pending. EV-0223 records a different, dictated reading of the farm name that this page does not show.
- Public record: EV-0224 — 1881 census, Llandough, RG11/5288 p.2 (photograph and transcription) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0224-1881-census-llandough-rg11-5288/
- Publication: Slater's Directory 1880, p.533, farmers in Llandough: "Williams John, Greathouse" (University of Leicester Historical Directories) — https://leicester.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/90316
- Publication: Owen's Cardiff Directory 1887, p.209: "Williams John, Great House farm, Llandough" (University of Leicester Historical Directories) — https://leicester.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16445coll4/id/92950
- Publication: EV-0225 — Trade directories 1868–1901: "Williams John, Great house" (wiki evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0225-trade-directories-1868-1901-john-williams-great-house/
- Newspaper: EV-0228 — Llandough Farm and the Rees family, 1841–1910: a separate Bute farm (wiki evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0228-llandough-farm-rees-family-1841-1910/
- Wiki page: EV-0223 — 1881 census: a dictated variant of the farm name (pending) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0223-1881-census-name-variant/

### I.8 (20). 15 December 1887 (obituary) — Death of Daniel Thomas

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18871215-1 · Date: 1887-12-15 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Newspaper

Daniel Thomas of Penylan dies. His obituary in Tarian y Gweithiwr describes him as a contractor under Lord Bute and the owner of "valuable lime kilns at Llandough". In April 1888 a local man is described as "a labourer at Llandough Quarry": the quarry beside the farm is still worked.

> What we now know: Daniel Thomas held the Llandough lime kilns under the 1877 arrangement with Bute; the works passed to his family and continued after his death.
- Newspaper: EV-0280 — Llandough lime works and quarry, 1876–1947: Daniel Thomas’s kilns and quarry workers — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0280-llandough-lime-works-and-quarry-1876-1947-daniel-thomas-s-kilns-quarry-workers-kel/

### I.9 (21). 11 August 1889 — Apples from the orchard

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18890811-1 · Date: 1889-08-11 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Newspaper

Four boys climb "over the hedge from the railway" into "the orchard of Great House Farm" and take apples, "the property of John Williams". John Williams junior helps the constable catch three of them, and tells the Penarth magistrates that about half the apples in his father's orchard have gone.

> The received account: A minor court report.
> Wording: "the property of John Williams" — The apples were his; the report is silent on who owned the land.
> What we now know: VERIFIED (Barry Dock News, 16 August 1889, read on Welsh Newspapers Online; EV-0279). Contemporary record that John Williams held Great House Farm in 1889, with his grown son John Williams junior working it, and that the orchard lay against a railway hedge.
- Newspaper: EV-0279 — Barry Dock News, 16 August 1889, p.2: "the orchard of Great House Farm … the property of John Williams" (wiki evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0279-barry-dock-news-16-aug-1889-p-2-apples-taken-from-the-orchard-of-great-house-farm/
- Newspaper: Barry Dock News, 16 August 1889, p.2 — "A Batch of Orchard Looters at Llandough" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/4594680/4594682/18/

### I.10 (22). 11 November 1891 — Theft of geese

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18911111-1 · Date: 1891-11-11 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Newspaper

Three geese are taken from "Mr. John Williams, Great House Farm, Llandough". The theft is reported from court.

> The received account: A minor court report.
> What we now know: Contemporary proof that John Williams lived at the house in 1891.
- Newspaper: 1891 court report — farmyard theft — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/press-archive-transcripts/#n01
- Newspaper: South Wales Star, 10 June 1892 — geese "the property of Mr. John Williams, Great House Farm, Llandough, on November 11, 1891" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3019697/3019705/78/
- Newspaper: EV-0226 — South Wales Star, 10 June 1892: "Mr. John Williams, Great House Farm, Llandough" (wiki evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0226-south-wales-star-1892-john-williams-great-house-farm/

### I.11 (23). 1892 — Signals across the water: Preece at Lavernock

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18920101-1 · Date: 1892-01-01 · Parcel: Not Great House Farm land · Basis: Newspaper

The Post Office engineer William Preece stretches long parallel wires on the shore at Lavernock and on Flat Holm, 3.3 miles out, and sends messages between them by induction, with no wire across the water. Five years later Marconi comes to the same shore.

> What we now know: VERIFIED that the 1892 messages were reported in 1897 in Preece's own words (South Wales Daily Post, 5 June 1897). The details (wire lengths, 3.3 miles, the failed attempt to Steep Holm) are SECONDARY, from Fahie's history of 1899/1901. This is the Lavernock background to Marconi.
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] South Wales Daily Post, 5 June 1897, p.3 — Preece's Royal Institution lecture: "In 1892 distinct messages were sent across a portion of the Bristol Channel between Penarth and the Flat Holm, a distance of over three miles" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3356360/3356363/20/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Cardiff Times, 13 March 1897, p.2 — "No Use for Wires": the "wonderful doings" of Mr Preece "at Lavernock and the Flat Holm" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3431204/3431206/41/
- Publication: [SECONDARY] J. J. Fahie, A History of Wireless Telegraphy (1899; 2nd ed. 1901), chapter on Preece's induction method: the Lavernock–Flat Holm trials — https://earlyradiohistory.us/1901fa21.htm

### I.12 (24). Week of 30 July 1894 — Swine fever at Great House

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18940731-1 · Date: 1894-07-31 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Newspaper

Swine fever breaks out at Llandough. Five pigs belonging to Mr Williams of Great House are slaughtered. On the Tuesday morning one of his herd of 23 is reported affected, and it is feared the whole herd will have to go.

> What we now know: VERIFIED (two newspapers, 3 August 1894). Most likely the John Williams whom the directories place at Great House Farm, Llandough (1868–1901). Against it: there is another Great House at Llandough near Cowbridge, and the report pairs Llandough with Rhoose, so the parish is not certain. The herd of 22–23 pigs shows a working farm.
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Barry Dock News, 3 August 1894, p.5 — "Swine fever at Llandough and Rhoose": "Five pigs belonging to Mr Williams, Great House, have been slaughtered" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/4596799/4596804/24/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Glamorgan Gazette, 3 August 1894, p.5 — the same report (herd given as 22) (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3874190/3874195/53/
- Newspaper: EV-0247 — the swine-fever reports on the wiki (evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0247-barry-dock-news-1894-swine-fever-great-house-llandough/

### I.13 (25). Late April – early May 1897 — Marconi comes to Lavernock

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18970501-1 · Date: 1897-05-01 · Parcel: Not Great House Farm land · Basis: Newspaper

The Cardiff papers announce that the young Italian Guglielmo Marconi, 23, will come to Cardiff "in a few weeks" to signal across the Bristol Channel without wires, with the Post Office's staff and apparatus at his disposal. At Lavernock Point the receiving station goes up on the cliff: a tall pole with a zinc cylinder at the top (120 feet in the Evening Express; 30 yards in Preece's account). The press names the man who put it up only as "Mr. Williams (of the engineering department, Cardiff)". The sending station is on Flat Holm.

> The received account: Marconi's Welsh trials were a Post Office affair.
> Wording: "Mr. Williams (of the engineering department, Cardiff)" — The only Williams in any 1897 report read. He is a Post Office engineer in Cardiff. No initial or address is given.
> What we now know: VERIFIED: the trials, the date (Evening Express, 15 May 1897, p.4) and "Mr. Williams (of the engineering department, Cardiff)". The wiki's undated cutting EV-0011 is that Evening Express report; the same text is in the Western Mail of the same day. Sion Buckler's position (request to The National Archives, 16 July 2026) is that this Mr Williams was his forebear Mr Williams of Great House Farm, that Marconi stayed with the family at the farm in 1897, and that Thomas Williams of Great House carted Marconi's equipment. Link to Great House: evidence being added. The photograph that the wiki's Media Gallery captioned "Marconi wireless telegraph at Great House Farm" (caption corrected 19 October 2026) is the Flat Holm photograph of 13 May 1897 (see 13 May). Next records: Post Office establishment books (BT Archives, POST 59) for a Williams in the Cardiff engineering district in 1897; the 1901 census.
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Evening Express, 26 April 1897, p.2 — "Wireless Telegraphy … Coming to Cardiff in a Few Weeks to Experiment Across the Bristol Channel" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3270301/3270303/28/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Weekly Mail, 1 May 1897, p.4 — the same report (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3370882/3370886/79/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Evening Express, 15 May 1897 (Extra Special), p.4 — "Wireless Telegraphy. Marconi Invention Tested at Lavernock" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3270811/3270815/108/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Western Mail, 15 May 1897, p.6 — "Telegraphy without wires. Marconi invention tested at Lavernock" (same report) (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/4313747/4313753/61/
- Newspaper: EV-0011 — the same cutting on the wiki (catalogued there as undated; identified here as the Evening Express, 15 May 1897, p.4) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0011-marconi-lavernock-wireless-cutting-1897/
- Publication: [SECONDARY] J. J. Fahie, A History of Wireless Telegraphy (1899; 2nd ed. 1901), chapter on Marconi's method, drawing on Preece's Royal Institution lecture of 4 June 1897 — https://earlyradiohistory.us/1901fa23.htm
- Official correspondence: Sion Buckler, records request to The National Archives, 16 July 2026, "Mr. Williams, Cardiff Post Office Engineering Department, 1897 Marconi Lavernock Experiments" (TNA replied 30 July 2026 that it is not the right place to ask) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/?p=5363
- Newspaper: EV-0248 — Marconi in Wales, April–July 1897: the contemporary press record on the wiki (evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0248-marconi-in-wales-may-1897-contemporary-press/

### I.14 (26). 10 May 1897 — Preece's method tried again

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18970510-1 · Date: 1897-05-10 · Parcel: Not Great House Farm land · Basis: Publication

Before Marconi's own trials begin, the Post Office repeats Preece's induction method between Lavernock and Flat Holm. It works.

> What we now know: SECONDARY (Fahie, 1899/1901, from Preece's account). No 1897 newspaper read here mentions 10 May.
- Publication: [SECONDARY] J. J. Fahie, A History of Wireless Telegraphy (1899; 2nd ed. 1901), chapter on Marconi's method, drawing on Preece's Royal Institution lecture of 4 June 1897 — https://earlyradiohistory.us/1901fa23.htm
- Publication: [SECONDARY] BBC Wales History blog, "Marconi's Welsh wireless revolution" (May 2012), quoting the same account — https://www.bbc.co.uk/blogs/waleshistory/2012/05/marconi_wireless_open_sea_lavernock_point_flat_holm.html
- Diary: EV-0256 — George Kemp’s diary, 6–15 May 1897 (Bodleian MS. Marconi 89, extracts quoted by G. R. M. Garratt): Lavernock p — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0256-kemp-diary-lavernock-1897-bodleian-ms-marconi-89/

### I.15 (27). 11–12 May 1897 — Two days of failure

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18970511-1 · Date: 1897-05-11 · Parcel: Not Great House Farm land · Basis: Newspaper

Marconi's first attempts to receive signals from Flat Holm at the Lavernock cliff-top station fail. The Evening Express reports that the experiments on Tuesday "were not so successful as might have been desired".

> What we now know: VERIFIED that Tuesday 11 May went badly (Evening Express, 15 May 1897). Fahie says 11 and 12 May both failed, but the Evening Express calls Wednesday and Thursday "most satisfactory". The 1947 plaque gives 11 May as the day messages were first exchanged with Flat Holm. The sources conflict on 11–13 May.
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Evening Express, 15 May 1897 (Extra Special), p.4 — "Wireless Telegraphy. Marconi Invention Tested at Lavernock" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3270811/3270815/108/
- Publication: [SECONDARY] J. J. Fahie, A History of Wireless Telegraphy (1899; 2nd ed. 1901), chapter on Marconi's method, drawing on Preece's Royal Institution lecture of 4 June 1897 — https://earlyradiohistory.us/1901fa23.htm
- Heritage record: [SECONDARY] Rotary Club of Cardiff plaque, St Lawrence's churchyard, Lavernock (transcription): "BETWEEN LAVERNOCK AND FLAT HOLM 11th MAY, LAVERNOCK AND BREAN DOWN 18th MAY 1897 … ERECTED BY THE ROTARY CLUB OF CARDIFF 1947" — https://readtheplaque.com/plaque/marconi-s-first-radio-transmissions-across-water

### I.16 (28). 13 May 1897 — Signals across the sea

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18970513-1 · Date: 1897-05-13 · Parcel: Not Great House Farm land · Basis: Newspaper

The receiver is carried down to the beach below the cliff and joined to the pole by another 20 yards of wire. Signals from Flat Holm, 3.3 miles away, now print clearly on the Morse inker at Lavernock. The Evening Express reports that on Wednesday and Thursday "the results were most satisfactory". Watching are Preece, his second engineer Mr Gavey (late of Cardiff), the Cardiff postmaster Mr Fardo and other officials. The German Professor Slaby is there too.

> The received account: Marconi sent the first radio message over open sea, from Lavernock to Flat Holm, on 13 May 1897.
> Wording: "Are you ready?" — A later account of the first words. Another later account gives "CAN YOU HEAR ME" and "YES LOUD AND CLEAR". No 1897 source read here records the words.
> What we now know: VERIFIED: success by midweek (Evening Express: Wednesday 12 and Thursday 13 May "most satisfactory"); Preece, Gavey and Fardo present. SECONDARY: the date 13 May, the 20 extra yards of wire, and Slaby's presence (Fahie). Direction: in Preece's account (via Fahie) Flat Holm sent and Lavernock received; some modern accounts reverse it. The photograph is captioned by its source as Flat Holm, 13 May 1897. Its date and place rest on that caption. Link to Great House: evidence being added.
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Evening Express, 15 May 1897 (Extra Special), p.4 — "Wireless Telegraphy. Marconi Invention Tested at Lavernock" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3270811/3270815/108/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Western Mail, 15 May 1897, p.6 — "Telegraphy without wires. Marconi invention tested at Lavernock" (same report) (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/4313747/4313753/61/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] South Wales Echo, 17 May 1897, p.2 — "The Man About Town": "Lavernock and the Flat Holm will stand out in the history of electrical science"; the messages were recorded, not just heard (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/4604986/4604988/5/
- Publication: [SECONDARY] J. J. Fahie, A History of Wireless Telegraphy (1899; 2nd ed. 1901), chapter on Marconi's method, drawing on Preece's Royal Institution lecture of 4 June 1897 — https://earlyradiohistory.us/1901fa23.htm
- Photograph: [SECONDARY: date and place as captioned by the source] Post Office engineers inspect Marconi's apparatus on Flat Holm, 13 May 1897. Photo: Cardiff Council Flat Holm Project, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons (File:Post_Office_Engineers.jpg) — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Post_Office_Engineers.jpg
- Publication: [SECONDARY — conflicting] Later accounts give the first words as "Are you ready?" (We Are Cardiff, 13 May 2016) or "CAN YOU HEAR ME" / "YES LOUD AND CLEAR" (BBC Wales History, 2012). No 1897 source read here gives the words. — https://wearecardiff.co.uk/2016/05/13/marconis-first-wireless-message-transmitted-over-sea-from-flat-holm-to-lavernock-point/

### I.17 (29). 14 May 1897 (Friday) — The demonstration at Lavernock

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18970514-1 · Date: 1897-05-14 · Parcel: Not Great House Farm land · Basis: Newspaper

On Friday afternoon Marconi gives a semi-public demonstration. A select company of local scientists and engineers watches his system explained in miniature, with a transmitter facing a receiver about twenty yards away, and messages written by the Morse self-inker without a connecting wire.

> What we now know: VERIFIED (Evening Express, 15 May 1897; Carnarvon and Denbigh Herald, 21 May 1897). The guests are not named.
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Evening Express, 15 May 1897 (Extra Special), p.4 — "Wireless Telegraphy. Marconi Invention Tested at Lavernock" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3270811/3270815/108/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Carnarvon and Denbigh Herald, 21 May 1897, p.4 — "Telegraphing without wires": Preece "during last week" testing Marconi's invention between Lavernock Point and the Flat Holme; a select company of local scientists and engineers invited (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3603309/3603313/23/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Weekly Mail, 22 May 1897, p.8 — "Wireless Telegraphy. Marconi Invention Tested at Lavernock" (same report) (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3370921/3370929/162/

### I.18 (30). 18 May 1897 — Lavernock to Brean Down

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18970518-1 · Date: 1897-05-18 · Parcel: Not Great House Farm land · Basis: Newspaper

The range is pushed across the whole Channel. A message sent from Lavernock Point, through a wire carried 220 feet up on a kite, is received at Brean Down, near Weston-super-Mare, about eight and a half miles away. Marconi signs the paper tape. That week he works on Brean Down with Preece and Gavey.

> What we now know: VERIFIED: the 18 May date, the kite at 220 ft and Marconi's signature are all on the framed tape, as transcribed by the South Wales Echo on 27 May 1897. The Echo of 20 May has messages going from Brean Down to Lavernock that week; the tape reads Lavernock to Brean Down. Fahie dates the Brean Down link to the day after the Flat Holm success. Brean Down is in Somerset and is included only as the far end of the Welsh link.
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] South Wales Echo, 27 May 1897, p.4 — "First wireless telegram": "Sent from Lavernock Point through a kite at an elevation of 220ft., and received at Brean Down, May 18th, 1897 … (Signed) G. Marconi" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/4605031/4605035/99/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] South Wales Echo, 20 May 1897, p.3 — "The Marconi experiments": Marconi, with Mr Preece and Mr Gavey, "has this week been at work on Brean Down" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/4605001/4605004/57/
- Heritage record: [SECONDARY] Rotary Club of Cardiff plaque, St Lawrence's churchyard, Lavernock (transcription): "BETWEEN LAVERNOCK AND FLAT HOLM 11th MAY, LAVERNOCK AND BREAN DOWN 18th MAY 1897 … ERECTED BY THE ROTARY CLUB OF CARDIFF 1947" — https://readtheplaque.com/plaque/marconi-s-first-radio-transmissions-across-water
- Publication: [SECONDARY] J. J. Fahie, A History of Wireless Telegraphy (1899; 2nd ed. 1901), chapter on Marconi's method, drawing on Preece's Royal Institution lecture of 4 June 1897 — https://earlyradiohistory.us/1901fa23.htm

### I.19 (31). Late May – July 1897 — The first wireless telegram goes on show

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-18970527-1 · Date: 1897-05-27 · Parcel: Not Great House Farm land · Basis: Newspaper

The framed tape of the Brean Down message goes on view in the hall of the Cardiff Central Free Library. Work at Lavernock goes on "for a few days longer". On 4 June Preece describes the Penarth–Brean Down signals to the Royal Institution in London. Marconi leaves England for Italy on Monday 5 July 1897.

> What we now know: VERIFIED. Not found: the day Marconi left South Wales. The last Welsh press notice of the work found is the South Wales Echo of 20 May 1897. In 1897 Marconi's next move was to London, and then Italy (Spezia trials, 10–18 July 1897, per Fahie).
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] South Wales Echo, 27 May 1897, p.4 — the framed tape on view at the Cardiff Central Free Library (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/4605031/4605035/99/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] South Wales Echo, 20 May 1897, p.3 — "Work is still progressing at Lavernock, and will be continued for a few days longer" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/4605001/4605004/57/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] South Wales Daily Post, 5 June 1897, p.3 — Preece's Royal Institution lecture: signals "between Penarth and Brean Down … a distance of nearly nine miles" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3356360/3356363/20/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Carnarvon and Denbigh Herald, 9 July 1897, p.2 — Preece: "Marconi only left England on Monday" (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3603372/3603374/10/
- Newspaper: [VERIFIED] Y Negesydd, 23 July 1897, p.1 — "Pellebru heb wifrau": experiments "yn agos i Benarth, Caerdydd" by Mr Preece and Marconi (Welsh) (Welsh Newspapers Online) — https://newspapers.library.wales/view/3819134/3819135/2/

### I.20 (32). 29 November 1902 — Coppice woods offered at auction

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-19021129-1 · Date: 1902-11-29 · Parcel: Not yet known · Basis: Sale particulars

Stephenson & Alexander offer the Marquess of Bute's coppice woods at auction, including "Cwm Cydfin Wood, Leckwith and Llandough", the woodland north of the house (particular 192). The particulars do not state whether the land or only the coppice is offered.

> What we now know: The woodland north of the house was managed by Bute as coppice in 1902; whether the land itself changed hands then is not shown.
- Sale particulars: EV-0219 — Bute coppice woods sale, 1902: Cwm Cydfin Wood — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0219-bute-coppice-woods-sale-1902-cwm-cydfin-wood/

The Llandough Air-rifle Club holds its Easter Monday meeting at Great House Farm: ten shots at twenty yards. A Llandough man, J. Griffiths, comes third.

### I.22 (34). 1908 — John Williams

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-19080101-1 · Date: 1908-01-01 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Mary's statement

Mary's grandfather dies. John Williams takes over the house from the Thomases and the fields from Bute.

> The received account: John Williams became the tenant of the farm.
> Wording: "the tenant" — Singular, as if there were one tenancy of one farm.
> What we now know: Two tenancies from two landlords: Parcel A from the Thomases, Parcel B from Bute.
> Title move — Parcel A: the true title: Freehold: the Thomases · tenant: John Williams
> Title move — Parcel B: the fields: Freehold: the Bute Estate · tenant: John Williams

- Newspaper: EV-0283 — Bute Court Leet at Llandough 1904–1917: “John Williams” on the 1910 jury (wiki evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0283-bute-court-leet-at-llandough-press-reports-1904-1917-john-williams-on-the-1910-gra/

### I.23 (35). 6 January 1908 — A poacher caught on Great House Farm

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-19080106-1 · Date: 1908-01-06 · Parcel: Not yet known · Basis: Newspaper

Shortly before three in the morning two keepers on their round at Llandough see a man net two rabbits on Great House Farm and catch him before he leaves the field. At Barry he is sent to gaol for two months.

> What we now know: VERIFIED (Evening Express, 10 January 1908). The keepers are not said to be the farm's own. John Williams of Great House died later in 1908 (EV-0243).

### I.24 (36). 10 August 1913 — Birth of Mary (Nancy) Williams

Act I: Division · Scene id: ghf-19130810-1 · Date: 1913-08-10 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Mary's statement

Mary (Nancy) Williams is born in the farmhouse on 10 August 1913.

> The received account: A tenant's daughter.
> What we now know: The owner of Parcel A from 1928 by her family's title. She lived in the house until her death in 1983.
- Wiki page: Mary (Nancy) Williams — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/mary-williams/
- Mary's statement: Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement (c. 1974) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/mary-williams-statement/

### II.1 (37). February 1916 — The 1916 tenancy

Act II: Tenancies · Scene id: ghf-19160201-1 · Date: 1916-02-01 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Court record

Bute grants John Williams a yearly tenancy described as "the whole farm". The document has not been found.

> The received account: The Williamses were yearly tenants of the whole farm from 1916, and every later right flows from that tenancy.
> Wording: "the whole farm" — Quoted by the Court of Appeal in 1987 as the start of the history.
> Wording: "since 1916" — The European Commission's date for the family's occupation.
> What we now know: In 1916 Bute owned only Parcel B. It could not let the house, which Thomas owned. "The whole farm" is a landlord's description of land it did not own: the birth of a single, synthetic farm that existed only on paper. Every later case was fought over that synthetic farm.
> Title move — Synthetic Parcel A: Seed (a landlord's wording, not the family's): the words "the whole farm" in a Bute tenancy (Bute can only let Parcel B)

- Court record: The 1916 Tenancy — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1916-tenancy/#grant
- Court record: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/bp-properties-v-buckler/
- Wiki page: The Farm / Whole Farm Nomenclature — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/the-two-parcels/whole-farm-nomenclature/

### II.2 (38). 14 December 1927 — Death of Lord Pontypridd

Act II: Tenancies · Scene id: ghf-19271214-1 · Date: 1927-12-14 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Newspaper

Alfred Thomas, Lord Pontypridd, son of Daniel Thomas of the Llandough lime works, dies unmarried. The next year the last quarry machinery leaves and the final rent on the house is paid.

> What we now know: The death of Daniel Thomas's son and heir in December 1927 comes immediately before the 1928 end of quarrying and of rent on the house.
- Newspaper: EV-0284 — Alfred Thomas, Lord Pontypridd, son of Daniel Thomas of the Llandough lime works, dies 1927 — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0284-alfred-thomas-lord-pontypridd-son-of-daniel-thomas-of-the-llandough-lime-works-die/

### II.3 (39). 1928 — Last rent on the house

Act II: Tenancies · Scene id: ghf-19280101-1 · Date: 1928-01-01 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Mary's statement

Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement records that in 1928 the last quarry machinery left, and John Williams paid a final rent of about £4 to Alfred Thomas. She saw the receipt. It is missing.

> The received account: Nothing happened in 1928. The tenancy of the whole farm carried on.
> What we now know: On Mary's statement, the bargain of 1877 came due: the quarrying ended and the freehold of the house passed to the Williamses, and they never paid rent on it again. The wiki treats 1928 as the strongest evidence-based date for the Williams freehold. The freehold line of the house: the Vaughans, then Bute (by the early 19th century), then Daniel Thomas (1877), then the Williamses (1928).
> Title move — Parcel A: the true title: Freehold: the Williamses (Bute → Thomas → Williams; 1877 agreement and 1928 receipt kept at the house)

- Biography: EV-0284 — Alfred Thomas, Lord Pontypridd, died 14 Dec 1927; estate report (wiki evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0284-alfred-thomas-lord-pontypridd-son-of-daniel-thomas-of-the-llandough-lime-works-die/
- Mary's statement: Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement (c. 1974) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/mary-williams-statement/
- Wiki page: The 1877 Agreement — takes effect 1928 — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1877-agreement/#takes-effect
- Land Registry record: Land Registry Titles — deeds before registration (15 May 1924 agreement) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/land-registry-titles/#deeds-before-registration
- Analysis: Forensic Master Chronology (6 October 2026) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/forensic-master-chronology-authoritative-corrected-6-october-2026/
- Wiki page: The Two Parcels — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/the-two-parcels/

### II.4 (40). 1936 — Marriage

Act II: Tenancies · Scene id: ghf-19360101-1 · Date: 1936-01-01 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Newspaper

Mary (Nancy) Williams marries Frederick Buckler, who comes to live at the farmhouse. They have seven children. The Western Mail of 5 August 1936 reports the wedding of Mr. Fred Buckler of Barry and Miss Mary Doreen (Nancy) Williams of Great House Farm (snippet only).

> The received account: Frederick joined the tenant family on the farm.
> What we now know: Frederick married into the house, which was Mary's family's. His later tenancy was of the fields only.
- Newspaper: EV-0230 — Western Mail, 5 August 1936, p.10: "Llandough Bride", Buckler–Williams wedding (SNIPPET ONLY; wiki evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0230-western-mail-1936-llandough-bride-buckler-williams/
- Wiki page: Frederick Buckler — marriage — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/frederick-buckler/#marriage
- Wiki page: Frederick Buckler — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/frederick-buckler/
- Wiki page: The Williams / Buckler Family — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/williams-buckler-family/

### II.5 (41). 1938 — Sale to Western Ground Rents

Act II: Tenancies · Scene id: ghf-19380101-1 · Date: 1938-01-01 · Parcel: Fields (B) · Basis: Court record

The Bute Estate conveys its reversion on the 1916 tenancy to Western Ground Rents Ltd.

> The received account: Western Ground Rents bought the farm, and became the Williamses' landlord for all of it.
> Wording: "the reversion" — Read later as the reversion on the whole farm.
> What we now know: Bute could only convey what it owned: Parcel B and its landlord's interest in the fields. Western Ground Rents acquired no deed to Parcel A, then or ever.
> Title move — Parcel B: the fields: Freehold: Western Ground Rents (from Bute, 1938) · tenant: John Williams

- Newspaper: EV-0285 — Western Mail snippets 1925–1939: Great House Farm under John Williams (sheep 1925, pony 1937, gun lost Feb 1939) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0285-snippets-only-western-mail-1925-1939-naming-great-house-farm-llandough-john-willia/
- Wiki page: 1938–39: Sale to WGR and the Revised Tenancy — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1939-revised-tenancy/#y1938
- Court record: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/bp-properties-v-buckler/
- Archive catalogue: EV-0257 — Glamorgan Archives D696: Western Ground Rents Ltd records 1938–44 (a syndicate headed by Lord Kennet; Bute urb — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0257-glamorgan-archives-d696-western-ground-rents-records-custodial-history/
- Archive catalogue: EV-0262 — TNA LT 13/3048: Western Ground Rents Ltd v the Lord Mayor, Aldermen and Citizens of the City of Cardiff, Lands — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0262-tna-lt-13-3048-western-ground-rents-v-cardiff-lands-tribunal-1967/

### II.6 (42). May 1939 — The 1939 tenancy

Act II: Tenancies · Scene id: ghf-19390501-1 · Date: 1939-05-01 · Parcel: Fields (B) · Basis: Document

Western Ground Rents grants John Williams a revised tenancy, with a plan.

> The received account: A renewal of the farm tenancy.
> What we now know: The plan shows the fields east of the house only: Parcel B. The landlord's own document leaves the house out. It is the last written tenancy.
> Title move — Parcel B: the fields: Freehold: Western Ground Rents · tenant: John Williams (1939 plan: fields only)

- Wiki page: 1938–39: the 1939 tenancy — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1939-revised-tenancy/#y1939
- Wiki page: The 1939 tenancy plan — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1939-revised-tenancy/#plan

### II.7 (43). c. 1940 — Twelve years

Act II: Tenancies · Scene id: ghf-19400101-1 · Date: 1940-01-01 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Family case

By 1940, twelve years after 1928, no rent has been paid on the house.

> The received account: Not an event. The family were tenants throughout.
> What we now know: Twelve years' rent-free possession from 1928 gives the family title to Parcel A by possession by 1940, in addition to the 1877–1928 title. The wiki notes this depends on what title the Thomases held. On either footing, from 1940 there was no basis for treating the family's occupation of the house as permission from Western Ground Rents, which never owned it.
> Title move — Parcel A: the true title: Freehold: the Williamses, by the 1877 bargain and by title by possession (twelve years rent-free, 1928–1940)

- Wiki page: 1938–39 — c. 1940 — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1939-revised-tenancy/#c1940
- Analysis: Forensic Master Chronology (6 October 2026) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/forensic-master-chronology-authoritative-corrected-6-october-2026/

### II.8 (44). 1940 – April 1942 — The gift of Leckwith Woods

Act II: Tenancies · Scene id: ghf-19420401-1 · Date: 1942-04-01 · Parcel: Not yet known · Basis: Public record

Western Ground Rents gives about 109 acres of Leckwith Woods to Cardiff council. The gift is offered and accepted in 1940 and completed in April 1942. Whether it takes in any of the woodland beside the farm is a question for the 1942 conveyance plan.

> What we now know: The extent of the 1940–42 gift is not yet laid over the farm's boundaries; the 1942 conveyance and its plan would settle it.
- Archive catalogue: Cardiff Parks Committee minutes, 1940–42 (Glamorgan Archives BC/C/6/79) — https://canfod.glamarchives.gov.uk/en/records/BC/C/6/79
- Wiki page: Master Timeline — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/timeline/

### II.9 (45). 1944 — Farm management

Act II: Tenancies · Scene id: ghf-19440101-1 · Date: 1944-01-01 · Parcel: Fields (B) · Basis: Mary's statement

The War Agricultural Executive Committee is dissatisfied with the farm. Frederick Buckler takes over running it as manager for John Williams.

> The received account: The tenant farm was failing.
> What we now know: Frederick managed the fields, Parcel B.
- Newspaper: EV-0286 — Western Mail, 17 Nov 1942: farm stock sale at “Great House Farm, Llandough” (snippet; parish unverified) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0286-snippet-only-western-mail-17-nov-1942-p-2-important-sale-of-live-and-dead-farming/

### II.10 (46). 1947 — The Lavernock plaque

Act II: Tenancies · Scene id: ghf-19470101-1 · Date: 1947-01-01 · Parcel: Not Great House Farm land · Basis: Heritage record

The Rotary Club of Cardiff puts up a bronze plaque at St Lawrence's, Lavernock: "Near this spot the first radio messages were exchanged across water by Guglielmo Marconi and George Kemp."

> What we now know: SECONDARY: the plaque's wording is from a published transcription, and the BBC gives the unveiling as 1948. It names George Kemp.
- Heritage record: [SECONDARY] Rotary Club of Cardiff plaque, St Lawrence's churchyard, Lavernock (transcription): "BETWEEN LAVERNOCK AND FLAT HOLM 11th MAY, LAVERNOCK AND BREAN DOWN 18th MAY 1897 … ERECTED BY THE ROTARY CLUB OF CARDIFF 1947" — https://readtheplaque.com/plaque/marconi-s-first-radio-transmissions-across-water
