### VII.22 (126). 2 December 2005 — Woodland land sold

Act VII: Development · Scene id: ghf-20051202-1 · Date: 2005-12-02 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Company accounts

On 2 December 2005 Forest of Cardiff transfers land to Goldsworthy Homes, and on 22 December part of the woodland title is divided off. Forest of Cardiff's accounts for the year to 30 June 2006 record "Sale of Land — Leckwith Road, Llandough 20,000". Which land was sold is not known until the transfer plan is read.

> The received account: The woodland charity sold a piece of land at Leckwith Road.
> Wording: "Sale of Land" — The charity's own accounts. The land was not on its balance sheet.
> What we now know: HELD (EV-0217, Companies House). £20,000 received in the year to 30 June 2006. Which land, and how the charity came to hold it in 1994, are open questions.
- Company accounts: EV-0217 — Forest of Cardiff accounts to 30 June 2006, note 13: "Sale of Land — Leckwith Road, Llandough" (wiki evidence page) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence/ev-0217-forest-of-cardiff-accounts-2006-sale-of-land-leckwith-road/

### VII.23 (127). 20 March 2019 — 1990 assessment archived

Act VII: Development · Scene id: ghf-20190320-1 · Date: 2019-03-20 · Parcel: Not yet known · Basis: Heritage record

On 20 March 2019 GGAT's 1990 assessment is added to the national record.

### VIII.16 (143). September – October 2026 — HER source-file digitisation and publication

Act VIII: Records · Scene id: ghf-20261006-1 · Date: 2026-10-06 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Official correspondence

The public HER entry GGAT02038s already referred to H. J. Thomas's 1974 survey and cited R. F. Suggett's December 1988 note. Following the family's September 2026 records request, Heneb reportedly stated on 14 October that the underlying source file had been digitised and uploaded to Archwilio as PDFs in the sources section. Heneb responded to the schedule of records on 16 October. This distinguishes the earlier public citation from the later availability of the underlying source-file material; it does not by itself establish concealment or what the Strasbourg Commission received.

> What we now know: No deed has been produced by which Parcel A passed from the Williamses, or from anyone, to BP.

### O.1 (147). Plainly — They were not squatters

Stating the obvious: Stating the obvious · Scene id: ghf-obvious-01 · Parcel: n/a · Basis: Analysis

The Williams family lived at Great House from 1667 to 1988.

> The received account: A squatter was evicted after losing in court.
> Wording: "squatter" — How the case was understood in the press and in the street.
> What we now know: A squatter moves into a place that is not theirs. The Williamses were born in this house, married in it and died in it for three hundred and twenty-one years. On Mary's statement they owned it from 1928, and on the family's case by possession from 1940. Nobody who lives somewhere for three centuries is a squatter.
- Mary's statement: Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement (c. 1974) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/mary-williams-statement/
- Wiki page: The Williams / Buckler Family — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/williams-buckler-family/

### O.2 (148). Plainly — Mary never asked for permission

Stating the obvious: Stating the obvious · Scene id: ghf-obvious-02 · Parcel: n/a · Basis: Analysis

Mary (Nancy) Williams refused the tenancies offered in 1959 and 1965 and did not accept the 1974 letters.

> The received account: She lived there by the landlord's permission.
> Wording: "licence" — 1974; relied on in 1986 and 1987.
> What we now know: You cannot be given permission you refuse. Every offer of a tenancy, and the licence, was an attempt to turn an owner into a guest in her own house. She said no every time.
- Court record: The 1959 refusal — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1962-possession-order/#refusal-1959
- Wiki page: The 1965 offer — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1962-possession-order/#offer-1965
- Court record: The 1974 Licence Letters — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1974-licence-letters/#letters

### O.3 (149). Plainly — Nobody produced a deed to the house

Stating the obvious: Stating the obvious · Scene id: ghf-obvious-03 · Parcel: n/a · Basis: Analysis

No conveyance of the farmhouse parcel to Western Ground Rents or to BP, earlier than the 1975 conveyance between two BP companies, has been produced.

> The received account: BP owned the farm.
> Wording: "the paper title to the farm" — Court of Appeal, 1987.
> What we now know: If Western Ground Rents or BP had a deed to the house, they would have produced it at the first hearing and the case would have been over in a day. They used tenancy offers, orders, a licence and their own conveyance instead. People with deeds don't need tricks.
- Land Registry record: Land Registry Titles — deeds before registration — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/land-registry-titles/#deeds-before-registration
- Land Registry record: Land Registry Titles — conveyances — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/land-registry-titles/#conveyances

### O.4 (150). Plainly — They knew it was two parcels

Stating the obvious: Stating the obvious · Scene id: ghf-obvious-04 · Parcel: n/a · Basis: Analysis

In 1983 BP registered the farmhouse and garden as a separate title. In 1987 it was amalgamated with the main title.

> The received account: It was always one farm.
> Wording: "the whole farm" — 1916 onwards.
> What we now know: You cannot merge two titles unless there are two. BP knew. The Land Registry knew. The court read a separate conveyance of the farmhouse and garden. The only people never told what that meant were the family.
- Land Registry record: Land Registry Titles — first registration and amalgamation — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/land-registry-titles/#first-registration

### O.5 (151). Plainly — Losing on possession is not losing on ownership

Stating the obvious: Stating the obvious · Scene id: ghf-obvious-05 · Parcel: n/a · Basis: Analysis

The High Court (1986), the Court of Appeal (1987), the House of Lords (1988) and the European Commission of Human Rights (1989) ruled against the family on possession.

> The received account: They lost every case, so they must have been wrong.
> Wording: "lost" — Every headline.
> What we now know: They lost every round of an argument about who could live in the house. Nobody ever asked who owned it. You can lose a hundred times on the wrong question and still be right about the real one.
- Court record: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/bp-properties-v-buckler/
- Analysis: BP v Buckler: Scope, Decided & Undecided — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/scrutiny-and-accountability/court-judicial-issues/bp-v-buckler-scope-decided-undecided/

### O.6 (152). Plainly — William Buckler was the last obstacle

Stating the obvious: Stating the obvious · Scene id: ghf-obvious-06 · Parcel: n/a · Basis: Analysis

William Buckler was injured during the eviction of 29–30 November 1988, charged from hospital on 3 December, and bailed on 9 December on condition he stayed away from the site. The house was demolished on 6 December.

> The received account: A violent man was arrested and charged.
> Wording: "chainsaw farmer" — The headline.
> What we now know: He physically stood in their way, so he was removed: to hospital, to the dock, then barred from the site by his bail. With him out of the way there was nobody left between BP and the house. It came down within the week.
- Newspaper: South Wales Echo — 'Angry scenes as farmer evicted' — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/press-archive-transcripts/#n14
- Newspaper: South Wales Echo, 3 December 1988 (search extract GHF-E090-N15-06) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/press-articles-index/
- Newspaper: South Wales Echo, 9 December 1988 (search extract GHF-E090-N15-09) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/press-articles-index/

### O.7 (153). Plainly — Four in the morning was chosen

Stating the obvious: Stating the obvious · Scene id: ghf-obvious-07 · Parcel: n/a · Basis: Analysis

Listing was refused on 5 December 1988. Demolition began at about 4am on 6 December. The European Commission application was pending.

> The received account: An old building was cleared for housing.
> Wording: "suddenly and completely destroyed" — The Royal Commission's archive record (NMR 6048945).
> What we now know: You don't start bulldozers at four in the morning by accident. It was done in the dark, the morning after the last protection fell and before Strasbourg could be heard, so that it could not be stopped and could never be undone.
- Newspaper: 'Tears flow as 800 year-old farm house is razed at last' — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/press-archive-transcripts/#n11
- Heritage record: Historic Environment Record GGAT 02038s (Archwilio) — https://archwilio.org.uk/her/chi3/report/page.php?watprn=GGAT02038s

### O.8 (154). Plainly — The public was on their side

Stating the obvious: Stating the obvious · Scene id: ghf-obvious-08 · Parcel: n/a · Basis: Analysis

In 1974 about 1,000 people signed a petition to save the house. In 1988 villagers protested the demolition and an MP asked for the case to be reviewed.

> The received account: Nobody much cared about an old farmhouse.
> What we now know: The public stood with the family. A thousand signatures, an MP, a furious village. It made no difference. Where the public could not be persuaded, force and stealth were used instead.
- Newspaper: Daily Telegraph, 16 April 1974 — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/press-archive-transcripts/#n03
- Newspaper: South Wales Echo, 12 May 1988 (search extract GHF-E090-N15-03) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/press-articles-index/
- Newspaper: South Wales Echo, 7 December 1988 (search extract GHF-E090-N15-08) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/evidence-library/press-articles-index/

### O.9 (155). Plainly — The papers did not leave on their own

Stating the obvious: Stating the obvious · Scene id: ghf-obvious-09 · Parcel: n/a · Basis: Analysis

Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement records that the family papers were taken from the blanket box in 1950–52 by a lodger placed in the house by an estate agent, and given to the agent.

> The received account: If they ever had papers, they couldn't produce them.
> Wording: "never produced" — Court of Appeal, 1987.
> What we now know: Title deeds don't walk out of a blanket box. They were taken, by a man an estate agent put in the house, and handed to that agent. Thirty-five years later a court noted that they had never been produced.
- Mary's statement: Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement (c. 1974) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/mary-williams-statement/
- Wiki page: The 1877 Agreement — papers taken — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1877-agreement/#papers-taken

### O.10 (156). Plainly — A decision with no file

Stating the obvious: Stating the obvious · Scene id: ghf-obvious-10 · Parcel: n/a · Basis: Analysis

Cadw holds two photographs of 29 July 1988 and no other record of its 1988 listing consideration.

> The received account: Cadw assessed the house properly and it fell just short.
> Wording: "marginally below the bar" — Cadw, 2026.
> What we now know: A public body decided the fate of a three-hundred-year-old house and kept no file, no notes and no name. A decision nobody can examine is a decision nobody can challenge.
- Photograph: Cadw survey photograph of the farmhouse, 29 July 1988 (released 2026, ATISN 27021) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/records-access-chronology/foi-reply-register/#R37
- Analysis: Cadw — Forensic Critique — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/scrutiny-and-accountability/government-public-authority-involvement/cadw-forensic-critique-v8-0-0/

### O.11 (157). Plainly — They never asked a court who owned the house

Stating the obvious: Stating the obvious · Scene id: ghf-obvious-11 · Parcel: n/a · Basis: Analysis

BP's 1974 action, in which Mary pleaded ownership, was adjourned and not relisted. The 1984 writ sought possession, not a declaration of ownership.

> The received account: The courts settled who owned Great House Farm.
> What we now know: In 1974 the question of ownership was in front of a judge, and BP walked away from it. In 1984 it asked only for possession. If you were sure you owned the house, you would ask a court to say so. They never did.
- Court record: The 1974 Licence Letters — the action — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/1974-licence-letters/#action
- Court record: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler — the writ — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/bp-properties-v-buckler/#writ

### E.1 (158). Today — The sequence

Epilogue: Today · Scene id: ghf-99990101-1 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Analysis

1916 to 1987: a tenancy, two possession orders, three tenancy offers, licence letters, a conveyance, two registrations and an amalgamation.

> The received account: A landlord and its successors recovered their farm from tenants who stayed on without paying, and the courts confirmed it.
> Wording: "the whole farm" — 1916.
> Wording: "the whole of the farm" — 1955.
> Wording: "licence" — 1974.
> Wording: "the paper title to the farm" — 1987.
> Wording: "registered correctly" — 2026.
> What we now know: Parcel A was the family's from 1928, and by possession from 1940. It was never shown to belong to Western Ground Rents or BP. A synthetic single farm was described in 1916; six attempts (1949, 1955, 1959, 1962, 1965, 1974) treated Mary's occupation as permissive; the woodland and the land to the south were taken; the 1975 conveyance and 1983 registration gave the synthetic Parcel A a deed and a title; the 1987 amalgamation folded it into Parcel B. The courts decided possession and never decided ownership. Possession can be awarded without ownership being tried, and land can be registered without a rival claim being decided. Neither decides the older title.
- Wiki page: The Two Parcels — the title test — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/the-two-parcels/
- Court record: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/bp-properties-v-buckler/
- Land Registry record: Land Registry Titles — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/land-registry-titles/#first-registration
- Analysis: Legal Review — Fraud, Land and Human Rights — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/scrutiny-and-accountability/legal-review-fraud-land-human-rights/

### E.2 (159). Today — The two parcels in the record

Epilogue: Today · Scene id: ghf-99990101-4 · Parcel: Whole farm (A + B) · Basis: Analysis

Records of 1877–1987 describe the property both as one farm and as separate parts.

> The received account: It was always one farm, and nobody suggested otherwise.
> Wording: "the whole farm" — One farm.
> Wording: "the farmhouse and garden" — One part, named on its own.
> What we now know: Mary's 1974 statement describes the 1877 split; no lawyer of hers built a case on it. Western Ground Rents offered tenancies of, and sued for, the farmhouse and garden alone. BP conveyed it alone in 1975, registered it alone in 1983, and merged it in 1987. The Land Registry held two titles and joined them. The Court of Appeal read a conveyance of the farmhouse and garden. Those who knew the parcels were separate treated them as one where that helped and as two where that helped. The family's case is that this was a conspiracy against them.
- Mary's statement: Mary (Nancy) Williams's statement (c. 1974) — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/mary-williams-statement/
- Wiki page: The Two Parcels — the title test — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/the-two-parcels/
- Land Registry record: Land Registry Titles — two titles, then one — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/land-registry-titles/#first-registration
- Court record: BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2 — https://greathousefarmwiki.wordpress.com/bp-properties-v-buckler/

### E.3 (160). Today — The site today

Epilogue: Today · Scene id: ghf-99990101-2 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Analysis

Church View Close, twenty houses, stands on the site. The woodland is registered to the Forest of Cardiff. The human remains are held by the National Museum of Wales.

> The received account: A modern estate on a former farm.
> What we now know: The title to Parcel A has never been decided and never extinguished.

### E.4 (161). Today — Village history

Epilogue: Today · Scene id: ghf-99990101-3 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Public record

Llandough Community Council's page on the village's history describes the Roman villa and the 1994 burials. It does not mention Great House, the Williams family or the demolition.

> What we now know: There has been no public inquiry, apology or reparation.

### E.5 (162). Today — The family's requests

Epilogue: Today · Scene id: ghf-99990102-1 · Parcel: House parcel (A) · Basis: Family case

The family ask for: a ruling on the ownership of Parcel A; the return of the woodland and the green, or reparation; reparation for the houses built on the land; the return of the estate's artefacts; a true heritage record; and a public inquiry.

> What we now know: Every body involved is being given the opportunity to put it right before the family return to court.
